name: Soiling of glass
describes: City air lays a film on the weather face: soot (elemental carbon) absorbs light and soluble salts scatter it. Both saturate as the deposit grows. Rain washes a steep face partly clean; a sheltered or flat face keeps more. Glass has no pores, so the pore-scale term of the surface law is zero and all soiling is this film. Indoors, the same film comes from touch: fingerprints at hand height on vitrine faces.

terms.model: Favez et al. (2006), as quoted by Du et al. (2017): absorbed fraction X = 0.16 EC / (EC + 15), with EC the elemental carbon on the face in ugC/cm2; diffuse (scattered) transmittance Y = 0.28 ions / (ions + 64), with ions the soluble inorganic deposit in ug/cm2.

kinetics.text: Sheltered float glass in Paris soiled continuously over 1-24 months along a sigmoid (Hill equation) curve in deposited mass, carbon, soluble ions and haze.
kinetics.source: T. Lombardo, A. Ionescu, R. A. Lefevre, A. Chabas, P. Ausset, H. Cachier, 'Soiling of silica-soda-lime float glass in urban environment: measurements and modelling', Atmospheric Environment 39(6) (2005) 989-997, doi:10.1016/j.atmosenv.2004.10.030, https://hero.epa.gov/reference/126177/

touch.text: Coated (anti-reflective) faces are sold with an optional finish that 'repels fingerprints and dirt'; fingerprints are the vitrine's everyday soiling.
touch.source: SCHOTT AG, 'SCHOTT AMIRAN - Anti-Reflective Glass for Showcases', technical data sheet, version February 2022 (values to DIN EN 410; monolithic 4 mm; laminated 4/0.76/4 mm with PVB), https://media.schott.com/api/public/content/15fee70340c44e738fd4f24c40702d8c?v=35137cd2&download=true

photograph: A grey veil on the weather face of sloped glass, heaviest where water pools against glazing bars, with drainage streaks below them.
Fingerprints at hand height on vitrine faces.

unverified.reason: The Hill-equation parameters of Lombardo et al. 2005 (deposit against months) could not be read (ScienceDirect and HAL refused access), so the museum's deposit rate has no sourced number yet.
The CIBSE LG10 and BS 8206-2 tables of dirt loss by slope and location could not be read (the standards are paywalled; the web calculators do not print the values).
